name: The White Oak of Woodlawn

location.address: Woodlawn Cemetery, North Border Ave and Rutgers Ave, overlooking East 233rd Street

access: Free to walk in; Woodlawn Cemetery grounds open daily 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM (owner's page, woodlawn.org). Trees are trunk-labelled and mapped on the Woodlawn tree walk.
transport: 4 train to Woodlawn (terminus), beside the Jerome Avenue entrance; inside, check the cemetery map.
story: When New York drew up its first list of Great Trees in 1985, NYC Parks called this white oak the oldest tree in Woodlawn Cemetery. It is still one of the largest. The city measured its trunk at 64.2 inches across, a little over five metres round, with a height of about 27 metres and a crown 82 feet wide. Woodlawn's own arboretum page describes a massive white oak guarding the north edge of the cemetery, and counts it among 33 trees on the grounds with trunks five feet across or more. It stands at North Border and Rutgers Avenues, looking out over East 233rd Street. The title of oldest is no longer settled. In 2024 Parks added a black oak in Woodlawn's northeast corner and estimated it at nearly 300 years, without saying how the two compare. Nobody has published an age for this white oak at all, so the two claims sit side by side, one a ranking and one a number. If you know the history of either, tell us. The cemetery is free to walk in and open daily from 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM, and its trees carry trunk labels and appear on the Woodlawn tree walk map. Our pin uses the Parks coordinate and is approximate at cemetery scale, so use the map and the label to find the trunk.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, a little over five metres round, under a crown 82 feet wide, with a trunk label. It stands on the north edge of Woodlawn at North Border and Rutgers Avenues, above East 233rd Street.

name: The Weeping Beech of the Gould Plot

location.address: Woodlawn Cemetery, Jay Gould plot near the Gould Mausoleum

access: Free to walk in; Woodlawn Cemetery grounds open daily 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM (owner's page, woodlawn.org). Trees are trunk-labelled and mapped on the Woodlawn tree walk.
transport: 4 train to Woodlawn (terminus), beside the Jerome Avenue entrance; inside, check the cemetery map.
story: The Gould family built a mausoleum at Woodlawn, and the tree beside it has done a better job of looking permanent. This European weeping beech stands on the Jay Gould plot, near the Gould Mausoleum, and NYC Parks has listed it as a Great Tree since 1985. Parks describes twisting branches over a smooth, leathery trunk, and a canopy 63.5 feet across. Woodlawn lists a weeping European beech among the 33 trees on its grounds with trunks five feet across or more, which tells you the scale to expect. Its exact size is a small mystery. The Parks register carries the same figure, 53.3, in both its diameter and height columns, a copying slip that leaves neither number trustworthy. Nobody has published when it was planted either. The age of the mausoleum is not the age of the tree, and no source ties the two, so its age stays open. If you know, tell us. The cemetery is free to enter and open daily from 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM. Its trees carry trunk labels and are mapped on the Woodlawn tree walk, which is the surest way to find this one, since our pin is the Parks coordinate and only approximate. Come in autumn, when the hanging curtain of leaves turns gold and copper.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the weeping crown, 63.5 feet across, over a smooth trunk, with a trunk label. It stands on the Jay Gould plot, next to the Gould Mausoleum.

best_time.label: October and November, when the hanging curtain of leaves turns gold and copper

name: The Cutleaf Beech of the Woodbine Plot

location.address: Woodlawn Cemetery, Woodbine Plot, northeast of the Jerome Avenue entrance

access: Free to walk in; Woodlawn Cemetery grounds open daily 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM (owner's page, woodlawn.org). Trees are trunk-labelled and mapped on the Woodlawn tree walk.
transport: 4 train to Woodlawn (terminus), beside the Jerome Avenue entrance; inside, check the cemetery map.
story: At about 28 metres, this beech stands as tall as a nine-storey building, and its leaves look nothing like a beech's should. It is a cutleaf European beech, the unusual fine-leaved form that Woodlawn's arboretum page singles out among the 33 trees on its grounds with trunks five feet across or more. NYC Parks made it a Great Tree in 1985 and records it at 91 feet tall with a crown 50.5 feet wide. Parks offers a neat comparison. The bark is like that of the cemetery's weeping beeches, but the tree stands upright, without their drooping form. So you get the bark of a beech and a tall, conventional crown, and only when you look up at the leaves does the oddity show. It stands in the Woodbine Plot, northeast of the Jerome Avenue entrance, which makes it one of the first Great Trees you can reach after stepping off the 4 train at Woodlawn. One number on the register is best ignored. It gives a trunk diameter of 91.2 inches, which simply echoes the height figure in the next column. Nobody has published a planting date or an age. If you know when the Woodbine Plot was planted, or this tree's history, tell us. The cemetery is free and open daily from 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM, and its trees are labelled on the trunk and mapped on the Woodlawn tree walk. Our pin is approximate, from the Parks coordinate.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the finely cut leaves on an upright beech about 28 metres tall, with a trunk label. It stands in the Woodbine Plot, northeast of the Jerome Avenue entrance.

name: The White Pine by the Jerome Avenue Gate

location.address: Woodlawn Cemetery near the Jerome Avenue entrance

access: Free to walk in; Woodlawn Cemetery grounds open daily 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM (owner's page, woodlawn.org). Trees are trunk-labelled and mapped on the Woodlawn tree walk.
transport: 4 train to Woodlawn (terminus), beside the Jerome Avenue entrance; inside, check the cemetery map.
story: NYC Parks describes this tree with an honesty that registers rarely allow themselves. It calls its shape scraggly and twisted, the look of an old white pine, and then lists it as a Great Tree anyway, as it has since 1985. That is the case for it in one line. Woodlawn's own arboretum page names a native eastern white pine among its Great Trees, a local species holding its own among the European beeches and the Japanese umbrella pine on the same list. Its crown spreads about 48 feet. It is also the easiest of Woodlawn's listed trees to find. It stands near the Jerome Avenue entrance, the gate right beside the 4 train's last stop at Woodlawn, so you can see a Great Tree within a few minutes of leaving the platform. Beyond the crown, the record goes quiet. The Parks register puts the same number, 83.64, in both its diameter and its height columns, which cannot both be right, so neither is a measurement we can repeat. Nobody has published an age either, so old is the register's word and the only one we have. If you know its history, tell us. The grounds are free to walk in and open daily from 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM. Trees carry trunk labels and appear on the Woodlawn tree walk. Our pin, from the Parks coordinate, is approximate.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the scraggly, twisted shape of an old white pine, crown about 48 feet across, with a trunk label. It stands near the Jerome Avenue entrance, beside the Woodlawn stop of the 4 train.

name: The Umbrella Pine of Woodlawn

location.address: Woodlawn Cemetery, corner of Parkview and Chestnut Avenues, northeast of the Paterno mausoleum

access: Free to walk in; Woodlawn Cemetery grounds open daily 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM (owner's page, woodlawn.org). Trees are trunk-labelled and mapped on the Woodlawn tree walk.
transport: 4 train to Woodlawn (terminus), beside the Jerome Avenue entrance; inside, check the cemetery map.
story: A conifer from Japan has been one of New York's official Great Trees for forty years, at a cemetery crossroads in the Bronx. This Japanese umbrella pine stands at the corner of Parkview and Chestnut Avenues in Woodlawn Cemetery, northeast of the Paterno mausoleum, and NYC Parks has listed it since 1985. Parks calls it a unique conifer native to Japan, and records a crown only 22.5 feet across. Beside the 82-foot spread of Woodlawn's great white oak, that is modest. Size was never its argument. Woodlawn's own arboretum page names it among the cemetery's Great Trees, alongside native oaks and a white pine, as one of the plants that make these grounds an arboretum as much as a burial ground. The umbrella of the common name describes its needles, which radiate in whorls like the ribs of an opened umbrella, the single detail that makes it easy to pick out once you are at the right corner. Its other numbers are missing. The Parks register carries the same figure, 47.56, in both its diameter and height columns, a copying slip, so neither can be trusted. No planting date or age has been published. If you know when it went in, tell us. The cemetery is free and open daily from 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM, trees carry trunk labels, and the Woodlawn tree walk map shows where they stand. Our pin, from the Parks coordinate, is approximate.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the needles set in whorls like umbrella ribs, on a compact conifer with a crown about 22.5 feet across. It stands at Parkview and Chestnut Avenues, northeast of the Paterno mausoleum.

name: The Black Oak of Woodlawn's Northeast Corner

location.address: Woodlawn Cemetery, northeast corner

access: Free to walk in; Woodlawn Cemetery grounds open daily 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM (owner's page, woodlawn.org). Trees are trunk-labelled and mapped on the Woodlawn tree walk.
transport: 4 train to Woodlawn (terminus), beside the Jerome Avenue entrance; inside, check the cemetery map.
story: This oak was already old when Woodlawn Cemetery was laid out around it, and the planners decided to keep it. NYC Parks says the black oak in the cemetery's northeast corner was recognised as exceptional and preserved when the grounds were first designed, and it estimates the tree at nearly 300 years old. Parks does not say what that estimate rests on, so take it as the city's best judgement rather than a count of rings. If it holds, the tree started growing in the early 1700s, when New York was still a British colony. Woodlawn's arboretum page puts the trunk at six feet across, close to six metres round, and Parks calls it absolutely massive. It only joined the city's list of Great Trees in 2024, almost forty years after the first list named a white oak on the north edge of these same grounds as the oldest tree in Woodlawn. The two claims have never been reconciled. One is a ranking from 1985 with no age attached, the other an estimate from 2024 with no comparison. They stand about 330 metres apart, so you can judge both. If you know anything firmer about either tree's age, tell us. The cemetery is free to enter and open daily from 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM. Trees carry trunk labels and are mapped on the Woodlawn tree walk, which is the way to find this one; our pin, from the Parks coordinate, is approximate.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, about six feet across, on a black oak with a trunk label. It stands in Woodlawn's northeast corner, overlooking the Bronx, about 330 metres from the Great Tree white oak.

name: The Linden of Duke Ellington's Jazz Corner

location.address: Woodlawn Cemetery, Jazz Corner, overlooking the Duke Ellington family lot

access: Free to walk in; Woodlawn Cemetery grounds open daily 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM (owner's page, woodlawn.org). Trees are trunk-labelled and mapped on the Woodlawn tree walk.
transport: 4 train to Woodlawn (terminus), beside the Jerome Avenue entrance; inside, check the cemetery map.
story: Duke Ellington chose his grave for a tree. In 1959 he bought a family lot at Woodlawn Cemetery, drawn, NYC Parks says, by a stately linden, and he sketched the tree into his own plans for the memorial. The tree is a small-leaved lime, the species Americans call littleleaf linden, and it has become the centre of the cemetery's Jazz Corner. Around it are the memorials of Miles Davis, Lionel Hampton, Max Roach, Illinois Jacquet, Clark Terry and Coleman Hawkins. Few trees in New York keep company like that. Parks added it to the Great Trees list in 2024, and for once the reason on the register is not size. Parks gives no trunk measurement, height or age, and nobody else has published one, so we cannot tell you how big it is or how long it had stood before Ellington found it. If you know, tell us. What the record does say is that the tree came first. Ellington picked the spot because of it, and the corner grew around them both. Woodlawn Cemetery is free to walk in and open daily from 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM. Its trees carry trunk labels and are mapped on the Woodlawn tree walk, and the Ellington lot is the landmark to look for, since our pin is the Parks coordinate and approximate at cemetery scale. Come in early summer, when the linden flowers.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the linden overlooking the Duke Ellington family lot, with a trunk label. It stands at the centre of the Jazz Corner, among the memorials of Miles Davis, Lionel Hampton and Coleman Hawkins.

best_time.label: late June and July, when the linden over Ellington's lot is in flower

name: The Japanese Maple of Woodlawn

location.address: Woodlawn Cemetery, between Central Avenue and Spruce Avenue

access: Free to walk in; Woodlawn Cemetery grounds open daily 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM (owner's page, woodlawn.org). Trees are trunk-labelled and mapped on the Woodlawn tree walk.
transport: 4 train to Woodlawn (terminus), beside the Jerome Avenue entrance; inside, check the cemetery map.
story: Woodlawn Cemetery holds more than 300 old Japanese maples, and this one was chosen to speak for all of them. When NYC Parks added it to the Great Trees list in 2024, it named this tree as the representative of that whole population, planted across the cemetery in the 1900s. The detail Parks gives about how they got this way is the best part. The gardeners who planted them learned not to prune them. Parks describes this one as gnarled and sculptural, and it was picked to show what Woodlawn's maples have become. It is not even, strictly, a single tree. Parks says it was planted as a group of four. It stands between Central Avenue and Spruce Avenue in the cemetery. There is no measurement on the register, no height and no trunk size, and no planting year more exact than the 1900s, so its age is open. If you know when this group went in, tell us. A maple chosen out of three hundred deserves a slow look. Walk round it before you walk on, since a sculptural tree changes shape with every step. Woodlawn is free to enter and open daily from 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM. Its trees carry trunk labels and appear on the Woodlawn tree walk map, the surest way to find this one; our pin is the Parks coordinate and approximate at cemetery scale.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as a gnarled, sculptural Japanese maple grown from a group of four planted together, with a trunk label. It stands between Central Avenue and Spruce Avenue in Woodlawn Cemetery.

name: The American Elm of Wave Hill

location.address: Wave Hill, 4900 Independence Avenue, top of the lawn southeast of Wave Hill House

access: Paid entry: Wave Hill is a public garden, grounds open Tuesday to Sunday 10 AM to 4:30 PM (winter hours from 1 Nov), adults $10, students and seniors $6, free Thursdays (wavehill.org/visit, fetched 2026-11-03).
transport: Bx7 or Bx10 bus to West 252nd Street, then a walk to the garden gate; check route (not verified).
story: This elm stands about 35 metres tall, and in the 2000s it caught Dutch elm disease and lived. NYC Parks recorded it at 114.8 feet, with a trunk 57.1 inches across, a little over four and a half metres round, when it put the tree on its first list of Great Trees in 1985. It grows at the top of the lawn southeast of Wave Hill House in Riverdale, and Parks gives a precise tip for seeing it. Stand under the arbor of the Shade Border, where its vase-like shape shows best. Nobody knows quite how it got here. Wave Hill estimates it began growing in the early to mid-1800s, somewhere around two centuries ago, and says it may have been planted by the estate's owners or may simply have come up on its own. Those are two different stories for the same tree, and the garden has not chosen between them. Parks counts it a survivor of the disease. It does not stand alone. The same lawn holds a sugar maple that Parks puts close to 200 years and a lacebark pine that Wave Hill says went in in the early 1900s, both Great Trees too. Wave Hill is a public garden with paid entry, open Tuesday to Sunday, with free Thursdays; check wavehill.org for current hours. Our pin is the lawn coordinate Parks gives for all three, so it is approximate.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its height, about 35 metres, and its vase-like shape, seen best from the Shade Border arbor. It stands at the top of the lawn southeast of Wave Hill House, near a sugar maple and a lacebark pine.

name: The White Ash of the Bedford Park Gate

location.address: New York Botanical Garden, near the Bedford Park Boulevard entrance, overlooking Conservatory Drive

access: Paid entry: New York Botanical Garden is ticketed; check nybg.org for hours and prices (not fetched this pass).
transport: Metro-North Harlem Line to Botanical Garden station or the B/D to Bedford Park Boulevard; check route (not verified).
story: NYC Parks calls this tree a rare survivor of the emerald ash borer, and it stands by one of the gates of the New York Botanical Garden. It is a white ash at least 100 feet tall, with a trunk 47 inches across, about three and three-quarter metres round, and in 2024 the city added it to its list of Great Trees. It stands near the Bedford Park Boulevard entrance, overlooking Conservatory Drive. Its origin comes with a small puzzle. Parks describes it as a remnant of old New York hardwood forest. In the same entry it cites the garden's records, which say the tree was donated in 1907 by John Finley, the Foreman of the Gardeners. A donated tree and a forest remnant are hard to square, and the records do not say whether it was planted that year or arrived already grown. If the 1907 gift is the tree's start, it is about 120 years old. If it is older forest stock, it could be more. We give the gift date as the best documented figure and leave the rest open. If you know more of the Finley story, tell us. The garden is ticketed, so check nybg.org for hours and prices before you go. Our pin is the Parks coordinate and approximate, so head for the Bedford Park Boulevard gate and look up.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its height, at least 100 feet, and a trunk about 3.75 metres round. It stands near the Bedford Park Boulevard entrance of the garden, overlooking Conservatory Drive.

name: The Sycamore of the Everett Garden Gate

location.address: New York Botanical Garden, just northeast of the Everett Garden Gate

access: Paid entry: New York Botanical Garden is ticketed; check nybg.org for hours and prices (not fetched this pass).
transport: Metro-North Harlem Line to Botanical Garden station; check route (not verified).
story: Nobody planted this sycamore. NYC Parks says it seeded itself on the grounds of the New York Botanical Garden, so in a garden of chosen specimens, this one chose itself. It stands just northeast of the Everett Garden Gate, and its huge branches, Parks notes, shade the school groups that gather there. It has been measured at least twice. A site-wide tree survey by the WPA, the Depression-era public works programme, recorded the trunk at 46 inches across. When the city added the tree to its Great Trees list in 2024, it was 57 inches, about four and a half metres round. Eleven inches of trunk is the visible record of the decades between the two visits. What the survey said beyond that number is lost to us, since the sentence on the Parks page breaks off. We do not know when the tree came up, only that it was already big enough to log when the WPA crews came through, so its age is an open question. If the garden's archive dates it, tell us. The garden is ticketed, so check nybg.org for hours and prices. Our pin is the Parks coordinate and approximate. Look for the biggest spreading tree beside the Everett Garden Gate.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the huge spreading branches over a trunk about 4.5 metres round. It stands just northeast of the Everett Garden Gate, where school groups gather in its shade.

name: The English Elm of Stuyvesant Square

location.address: Western gate of Stuyvesant Square Park, Second Avenue side

access: Free; public park, open daily.
transport: L train to First Avenue or 6 to Astor Place, about 10 minutes' walk; check route (not verified).
story: This elm may be older than the park it stands in. NYC Parks thinks it was already growing here before 1836, the year Peter Gerard Stuyvesant gave this land to the city. Thought to, not known to. There is no planting record, and the claim is the register's own careful wording. If it holds, the tree was here first and the square came to it. Then there is the height. Parks measured it at 108.2 feet, about 33 metres, a tall tree by any standard and a striking one to find on a square in Manhattan. The trunk is slimmer than the height suggests, 42 inches across in the 1985 survey that first put it on the Great Trees list and 44 in the city's current forestry inventory, about 3.4 metres round. That inventory files it under Ulmus minor 'Atinia', the botanist's name for the English elm, and found it in Good condition in February 2026. For a tree that may have been standing here for close to two centuries, that is a decent report. It stands just inside the western gate, on the Second Avenue side of the square, free to visit whenever the park is open. If you know more about how old it really is, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its height, about 33 metres, on a trunk only 42 to 44 inches across. It stands just inside the western gate of Stuyvesant Square, on the Second Avenue side.

name: The Ginkgo of Isham Park

location.address: Isham Park, southeast corner at Broadway and West 211th Street

access: Free; public park.
transport: 1 to 215th Street or A to Inwood-207th Street, a few minutes' walk; check route (not verified).
verify_notes: Parks (1985): one of the best-known trees in the neighbourhood; 58 in diameter, 71.3 ft. Tree Map ID 5096375: forestry point dbh 58, Excellent, coordinates match. Pin confirmed by register tree-point.
story:
The parks department calls this ginkgo one of the best-known trees in its neighbourhood. It stands at the south-east corner of Isham Park, where Broadway meets West 211th Street, on a trunk 58 inches across, about 4.6 metres round, and about 22 metres tall. The city named it a Great Tree in 1985, and four decades later its forestry inventory records the same 58 inches and rates the tree excellent, the top grade it gives.

Ginkgo is the last survivor of a group of trees that was widespread when dinosaurs were alive, and it reached America only in the 1780s, as a garden curiosity in Philadelphia. Since then New Yorkers have planted it by the thousand, because it shrugs off salt, smog and compacted soil. Most of those street ginkgos are young and slim. This one shows what the species does when it is left alone in a park for a long time.

Isham Park was once part of the Isham family's estate in Inwood, given to the city in the early twentieth century. The ginkgo now holds its busiest corner, beside the traffic of Broadway, a few minutes' walk from the 1 train at 215th Street and the A at Inwood-207th Street.

Nobody has published when it was planted, or whether it went in before or after the land became a park. If you know, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its fan-shaped leaves, which turn butter yellow in autumn, on a trunk about 4.6 metres round. It stands at the south-east corner of Isham Park, at Broadway and West 211th Street.

best_time.label: November, when the fan-shaped leaves turn butter yellow and drop almost together

name: The Plane Tree of King's Bridge

location.address: East side of Corlear Avenue just south of West 231st Street

access: Free; street tree on Corlear Avenue.
transport: 1 train to 231st Street, then a walk toward Corlear Avenue; check route (not verified).
story: Close to this street corner in the Bronx, Washington's army crossed a bridge in retreat. NYC Parks puts the tree near the site of the King's Bridge, built by Frederick Philipse in 1693, and says that Washington's troops crossed it falling back after the loss of Fort Washington on 16 November 1776. The bridge is the history here; the tree is what still stands near where it was. Even the name of the tree is a small argument. Parks listed it in 1985 as an American sycamore. The city's own forestry inventory, which carries the same coordinates and the same 54 inch trunk, records it as a London plane, the hybrid of the American sycamore and the Oriental plane. We follow the inventory, and the two are close enough kin that a reader standing underneath may want to judge for themselves. Either way it is a big tree for a side street. The trunk is 54 inches across, about 4.3 metres round, and Parks measured it at 98.4 feet tall, about 30 metres. The inventory found it in Good condition in January 2024. It stands on the east side of Corlear Avenue just south of West 231st Street, a public street tree you can walk up to at any hour. Nobody has dated it. If you know when it went in, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 54 inches across, and the height, about 30 metres. It stands on the east side of Corlear Avenue just south of West 231st Street.

name: The Oak of U Thant's Forest Walk

location.address: Raoul Wallenberg Forest, off the Palisades Avenue hiking trail

access: Free; trail in Raoul Wallenberg Forest (Parks land) leaving Palisades Avenue 0.1 mile north of West 232nd Street; Parks directions: 500 ft up to the dead copper beech trunk, then 200 ft southeast. Hiking trail, uneven.
transport: 1 to 231st Street or Bx7 bus, then a walk to Palisades Avenue; check route (not verified).
story: The directions to this oak use a dead tree as a signpost. NYC Parks tells you to leave Palisades Avenue on the trail a tenth of a mile north of West 232nd Street, climb about 500 feet to the trunk of a dead copper beech, then go 200 feet southeast. There, in the Raoul Wallenberg Forest in Riverdale, stands a white oak that has been one of New York's Great Trees since the first list in 1985. Parks associates it with U Thant, the Burmese diplomat who was Secretary General of the United Nations from 1961 to 1971 and lived in Riverdale. The register does not say what the connection was, and we will not guess. If you know the story, tell us. The tree itself is big. Its trunk is 57 inches across, about four and a half metres round, and Parks puts it at 87.7 feet tall, about 27 metres. Nobody has published an age. Go soon, and go gently. The city's forestry inventory, which carries the same coordinates as the Parks listing, last recorded it in September 2023 and rated its condition poor. It was alive then, but that is the last word we have. The trail is a real hiking path, uneven underfoot, and entry to the forest is free. Our pin comes from the register's own tree record, so once you have found the dead beech, the oak is close.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, about 4.5 metres round, on a white oak 27 metres tall. It stands about 200 feet southeast of a dead copper beech trunk, 500 feet up the trail from Palisades Avenue.

name: The Green Ash of Crotona Park

location.address: Crotona Park, south of the Prospect Avenue entrance, behind the playground

access: Free; public park path between the soccer field and the playground.
transport: 2 or 5 to Freeman Street, then a walk to Prospect Avenue; check route (not verified).
story: This tree is on a medication schedule. NYC Parks treats the green ash behind the Crotona Park playground at regular intervals against the emerald ash borer, an insect that attacks ash trees, and so far the tree is holding up. When the city's forestry inventory last checked it, in September 2026, it rated its condition good. In 2024 Parks added it to its list of Great Trees and described its commanding presence on the path. The trunk is 55 inches across, about four and a third metres round. It stands south of the Prospect Avenue entrance, on the path between the soccer field and the playground, which gives one of the city's official Great Trees about as ordinary an address as a tree can have. Nobody has published when it was planted or how old it is, and we will not pick a number without a source. If you know its history, or remember it from decades of games on that field, tell us. Crotona Park has a second Great Tree, an American elm near the Claremont Parkway entrance, about 550 metres away, so the two make a short Bronx circuit, and both are free to visit. Our pin comes from the forestry inventory's own record of this tree, matched to the Parks listing, so it is confirmed.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, about four and a third metres round, on a green ash with a commanding presence over the path. It stands between the soccer field and the playground, south of the Prospect Avenue entrance.

name: The White Oak of the Property Line

location.address: Van Cortlandt Park, north side of Gun Hill Road at Mosholu Parkway North

access: Free; park edge on Gun Hill Road opposite the Mosholu Teaching Forest.
transport: 4 train to Mosholu Parkway, a walk; check route (not verified).
story: Somebody may once have planted this white oak to mark where their land ended. That is what NYC Parks believes, saying it went in hundreds of years ago as a property-line marker, though Parks gives no date, no names and no deed, so take the hundreds of years as a belief rather than a measurement. Nobody has recorded whose boundary it was. The tree outlasted the line. Its trunk now measures 58 inches across, about 4.6 metres round, on the north side of Gun Hill Road at Mosholu Parkway North, where Van Cortlandt Park meets the traffic. It joined the Great Trees list in 2024, the city's roll of its most remarkable trees, and its route there is a story of its own. It was not put forward by a forester or a historian but by an artist-in-residence working with the NYC Urban Field Station. An artist picked this one out of a park full of trees. The city's forestry inventory last recorded it in April 2023 and called it Good, with coordinates that match the Parks listing. It stands at the park's edge across Gun Hill Road from the Mosholu Teaching Forest, so it is easy to reach on foot and free at any hour, no trail walking needed. Nobody has dated it. If you know anything about the old line it marked, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 58 inches across, at the very edge of the park beside the road. It stands on the north side of Gun Hill Road at Mosholu Parkway North, opposite the Mosholu Teaching Forest.

name: The Mazzard Cherry of Ewen Park

location.address: Ewen Park, mid-park just south of the dog run

access: Free; public park.
transport: 1 train to 231st Street, a walk up the hill; check route (not verified).
story: One of the largest and oldest trees in Ewen Park is a cherry. NYC Parks says so in the entry that put this mazzard, the wild sweet cherry, on its list of Great Trees in 2024, and it is the kind of sentence that makes you look twice at a tree most people would pass for an ordinary flowering one. The trunk is 28 inches across, a little over two metres round, and Parks notes that it flowers in spring. It stands mid-park in Riverdale, just south of the dog run, so the likeliest company you will have while looking at it is somebody's dog. The city's forestry inventory last checked it in April 2025 and rated it in good condition, with coordinates that match the Parks listing exactly. Our pin comes from that record and is confirmed, which in a park full of trees is worth having. What nobody has written down is its age. Parks calls it one of the park's oldest without putting a number to it, and there is no planting date on record, so how long it has been flowering here is an open question. If you know, or have photographs of it from years back, tell us. The park is free and open to all, and the usual approach is from the 1 train at 231st Street. Come in spring if you can, when the cherry is in flower and the Great Tree label suddenly makes sense.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, a little over two metres round, on a cherry that flowers in spring. It stands mid-park, just south of the dog run in Ewen Park.

name: The Willow Oak of Herbert Street

location.address: In front of 86 Herbert Street

access: Free; Parks-inventoried street tree on the public sidewalk.
transport: L to Graham Avenue or Grand Street, a walk; check route (not verified).
story: In East Williamsburg, the biggest tree you can see for many blocks stands on the sidewalk in front of 86 Herbert Street. That is how NYC Parks describes it, and the people who live around it said so first. This willow oak became a Great Tree in 2024 after the community nominated it, the most direct way a tree can join the list. Somebody who passed it every day decided it deserved the city's attention, and the city agreed. Its trunk is 39 inches across, about three metres round, on an ordinary residential block. A willow oak is an oak that does not look like one. Its leaves are long and narrow, like a willow's, so from a distance this one could pass for the wrong tree entirely, and only the acorns give the family away. The city's forestry inventory last checked it in January 2026 and rated its condition fair, alive and holding. The coordinates on that record match the Parks listing, so our pin is confirmed. Nobody has published its age or planting date, and we will not guess one from the size. If you know when it went in, or remember the street before it was this big, tell us. It is a street tree on a public sidewalk, so it is free and always there. Stand across the street to take in the crown, and leave the front steps to the people who live behind it.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the biggest tree on the block, an oak with a trunk about three metres round and narrow, willow-like leaves. It stands on the sidewalk in front of 86 Herbert Street.

name: The Circus Ground Oak of Saratoga Park

location.address: Saratoga Park, south side of the path north of the children's playground

access: Free; public park.
transport: A or C to Utica Avenue, or J to Chauncey Street, a walk; check route (not verified).
story: Before Saratoga Park was a park, the whole block was a circus ground, and NYC Parks thinks this red oak likely dates from those days. Likely is their word, and it is worth keeping. There is no planting record and no ring count, only a tree big enough to make the idea plausible and a block with a history odd enough to make it memorable. The more recent history is better documented. When the park was renovated in 2023, the new playground was laid out around a central corridor to protect the tree, so the design bends to the oak rather than the other way round. In 2024 Parks added it to its Great Trees list, the city's roll of its most remarkable trees. The trunk measures 54 inches across, about 4.3 metres round, and the city's forestry inventory found it in Good condition in December 2025. It stands on the south side of the path just north of the children's playground, a public park tree you can walk right up to. If you know when it was planted, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 54 inches across, the big oak the playground was laid out around. It stands on the south side of the path just north of the children's playground in Saratoga Park.

name: The Shumard Oak of Sixth Avenue

location.address: 385 6th Avenue

access: Free; Parks-inventoried street tree on the public sidewalk.
transport: F or G to 7th Avenue or 4th Avenue-9th Street, a walk; check route (not verified).
story: Park Slope has changed around this oak, and the oak has stayed put. When NYC Parks named it a Great Tree in 2024, that was the reason it gave. The Shumard oak in front of 385 6th Avenue was chosen for standing the test of time while the neighbourhood transformed around it. It is a street tree, on a public sidewalk, with a trunk 47 inches across by the Parks listing and 48 by the city's forestry inventory, close to three and three-quarter metres round either way. The inch between the two is the sort of gap you get from two surveys at different times, not a dispute. Parks describes the Shumard as a fast-growing oak, which is worth keeping in mind before reading an age into that trunk. A fast grower reaches this size sooner than a slow one, so the girth does not translate neatly into years, and nobody has published a planting date. Its age stays open. If you know when it went in, tell us. What you can plan around is the colour. Parks notes that its leaves turn red to orange in autumn, which on a city street is the kind of thing people stop for. The forestry inventory last checked it in November 2025 and rated it in good condition, with coordinates matching the Parks listing, so our pin is confirmed. It is free and always there. Come in autumn, and look up from the sidewalk rather than the stoop.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, about 3.75 metres round, on a street oak whose leaves turn red to orange in autumn. It stands on the sidewalk in front of 385 6th Avenue in Park Slope.

name: The Umbrella Elm of West 1st Street

location.address: Near 1769 West 1st Street

access: Free; Parks-inventoried street tree on the public sidewalk.
transport: F to Avenue P or Bay Parkway, a walk; check route (not verified).
story: This American elm in Gravesend made New York's list of Great Trees for its shape. NYC Parks says it was selected in 2024 as a splendid tree with impressive form, and describes its crown as a nearly perfectly full umbrella. Not age, not fame, not a story. Just a street tree that grew into the outline a child would draw. The trunk is 51 inches across, a little over four metres round, which would be enough to notice it even without the shape. It stands on the public sidewalk near 1769 West 1st Street. The city's forestry inventory last checked it in February 2026, rated its condition good, and placed it at the same coordinates as the Parks listing, so our pin is confirmed. Nobody has published when it was planted or how old it is, so we leave the number blank. If you know the tree's history, or have an old photograph of the street with it in, tell us. Because the shape is the point, distance helps. Cross the street, or stand a few houses down, and the umbrella comes into focus in a way it never does from directly underneath. It is free, on a public sidewalk, and always there.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the crown, a nearly perfect umbrella, over an elm trunk a little over four metres round. It stands on the sidewalk near 1769 West 1st Street in Gravesend.

name: The Oak Moved from Prospect Park

location.address: 195 East 3rd Street

access: Free; Parks-inventoried street tree in front of a house, seen from the sidewalk.
transport: F or G to Ditmas Avenue or Fort Hamilton Parkway, a walk; check route (not verified).
verify_notes: Parks (2024): per the nominator and family legend, a former Parks worker took a small oak sapling from Prospect Park and planted it here in 1958 (legend, one family source); 50 in diameter, the largest tree for many blocks. Age derived from that 1958 planting story. Tree Map ID 1242920: Good, updated 2026-07-31, coordinates match. Pin confirmed by register tree-point. Earlier lead worried it stands in front of a home; the inventory records it as a Parks street tree.
story:
A former parks worker, the family story goes, walked out of Prospect Park in 1958 with a small oak sapling and planted it on East 3rd Street in Kensington. Today that northern red oak has a trunk 50 inches across, about four metres round, and the parks department, adding it to its Great Trees list in 2024, called it the largest tree for many blocks.

The story is a legend in the honest sense. It comes from the nominator and the family, one source, and nobody has a receipt for the sapling. But the tree fits it. A red oak planted in 1958 would be about seventy now, somewhere between 65 and 75 if the year is a little off, and red oak is among the faster-growing oaks of the eastern forest, so a trunk this thick in that time is plausible rather than miraculous.

If the legend holds, this is a piece of Prospect Park that moved a short way south. The park was laid out by Olmsted and Vaux in the 1860s, and one of its seedlings now shades a residential block instead, bigger than anything else on the street.

It stands in front of 195 East 3rd Street, and the city's forestry inventory records it as a street tree in good condition, last updated in July 2026. It is in front of somebody's house, so look from the sidewalk and let the house be. If you know more of the family story, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the largest tree for many blocks, a northern red oak about four metres round at chest height. It stands on the sidewalk in front of 195 East 3rd Street.

name: The Elm of 55th Avenue

location.address: 92-22 55th Avenue

access: Free; Parks-inventoried street tree on the public sidewalk.
transport: M or R to Grand Avenue-Newtown, a walk; check route (not verified).
story: There is an American elm in Elmhurst that stands taller than the houses on its street. NYC Parks says it towers above them, with a large spreading canopy, and in 2024 the city made it a Great Tree. The neighbourhood's name and the tree's species are a pleasing match, though no source we know of says the one has anything to do with the other, so enjoy the coincidence and leave it there. The trunk has two measurements that differ a little. The Parks listing gives 51 inches across. The city's forestry inventory, checked in June 2026, gives 54. That works out at somewhere around four metres round, and the three-inch gap is the ordinary result of different surveys at different times, not a quarrel about the tree. The inventory rated it in good condition, alive and well on a Queens sidewalk, and its coordinates match the Parks listing, so our pin is confirmed. It stands in front of 92-22 55th Avenue. Nobody has published its age or a planting date. If you know when it went in, or how the street looked before it outgrew the roofs, tell us. Because it is a street tree, it is free and always there, but the people behind it live there too. The best view of a canopy that tops the houses is from across the street or a little way down the block, where you can see how much sky it takes up.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the elm that towers above the houses, its trunk around four metres round under a large spreading canopy. It stands on the sidewalk in front of 92-22 55th Avenue.

name: The Willow Oak of Perry Avenue

location.address: 3331 Perry Avenue

access: Free; Parks-inventoried street tree on the public sidewalk.
transport: 4 train to Mosholu Parkway or D to Norwood-205th Street, a walk; check route (not verified).
story: This oak grew a trunk 55 inches across in a strip of ground that NYC Parks itself calls narrow and congested. That was the case for nominating it. When the willow oak in front of 3331 Perry Avenue in Norwood became a Great Tree in 2024, Parks said it was put forward for its size despite its growing conditions, which is the official way of saying it had no business getting this big where it is. Fifty-five inches across is about four and a half metres round. For comparison, the Herbert Street willow oak in Brooklyn, another Great Tree of the same species chosen the same year, is 39 inches. This one is the larger by a wide margin. The city's forestry inventory last checked it in April 2025, rated its condition good, and gives coordinates that match the Parks listing, so our pin is confirmed. Willow oaks carry narrow, willow-shaped leaves rather than the lobed ones most people picture on an oak, so look for the size first and the leaves second. Nobody has published its age or when it was planted. If you know, or have lived on Perry Avenue long enough to remember it smaller, tell us. It is a street tree on a public sidewalk, free and always there.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, about 4.5 metres round, on a willow oak squeezed into a narrow sidewalk strip. It stands in front of 3331 Perry Avenue in Norwood.

name: The Weeping Beech of Cypress Hills National Cemetery

location.address: Cypress Hills National Cemetery, 625 Jamaica Avenue, north of Norwood Avenue at Jamaica Avenue

access: Free; national cemetery open to visitors, listed by VA as open daily 8:00 AM to 4:30 PM (VA page via a 2013 archive snapshot, confirm).
transport: J to Norwood Avenue, a short walk to Jamaica Avenue; check route (not verified).
story: This weeping beech spreads over a burial ground of more than 21,000 veterans and their dependents, 24 of them holders of the Medal of Honor. NYC Parks describes the beech at Cypress Hills National Cemetery as far-reaching, hovering over those graves, and in 2024 it made the tree a Great Tree. Cypress Hills is, by the Parks account, the only national cemetery in New York City, which gives a single tree here an unusual charge. It is a European weeping beech, a cultivated form whose branches hang rather than reach, planted in a place built for remembering. The register gives no measurements, no trunk size, no height and no age, and nobody else has published them, so the story here is the setting rather than the numbers. If you know when the beech was planted, or have measured it, tell us. Visiting needs a little care. The cemetery is free and open to visitors, and the Department of Veterans Affairs has listed it as open daily from 8:00 AM to 4:30 PM, but that listing comes from an older copy of its page, so confirm the hours before you go. It is a working national cemetery, and the people at the graves may be there for their own family. Our pin is the Parks coordinate and approximate at cemetery scale, north of Norwood Avenue at Jamaica Avenue. Come in autumn, when the hanging curtain of leaves turns gold and copper over the stones.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the far-reaching weeping crown that hangs over the graves. It stands in Cypress Hills National Cemetery, north of Norwood Avenue at Jamaica Avenue, at 625 Jamaica Avenue.

best_time.label: October and November, when the hanging curtain of leaves turns gold and copper over the graves
